questions.explain: Server Audit defines where audit records go, Server Audit Specification captures server-level events (logins, role changes), and Database Audit Specification captures database-level events (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on specific objects).
options: Server Audit → Server Audit Specification → Database Audit Specification.
Error Log → Extended Events → Query Store.
Login auditing → role auditing → object auditing.
Agent job → Database Mail → audit file.
questions.q: What are the three layers of SQL Server's audit framework?

questions.explain: CONTINUE lets the server keep running unaudited when the audit target is unavailable; SHUTDOWN stops the instance to prevent unaudited operations. Regulated environments often require SHUTDOWN, but a full disk or unavailable share will then bring down the instance.
options: CONTINUE retries writing to the audit target forever.
ON_FAILURE = CONTINUE lets the server run unaudited if the audit target is unavailable, while SHUTDOWN stops the instance — a serious decision for regulated environments.
SHUTDOWN only affects the auditing database, not the instance.
ON_FAILURE applies only to the Error Log, not to audit files.
questions.q: In CREATE SERVER AUDIT, what is the difference between ON_FAILURE = CONTINUE and ON_FAILURE = SHUTDOWN?

questions.explain: Profiler/server-side Trace imposes server-side tracing overhead that can cripple a busy production system; Extended Events is the lightweight, high-performance framework that replaced it — always with a predicate on high-frequency events so it doesn't write gigabytes per hour.
options: They write events to the same .xel file format.
Never run Profiler or server-side Trace on production — the overhead can cripple a busy system; use Extended Events instead, always with a predicate on high-frequency events.
Extended Events cannot capture slow queries, only Profiler can.
Profiler is required for auditing login failures.
questions.q: Why does the chapter say to never run SQL Server Profiler or server-side Trace on production?

questions.explain: Audit files are queried with sys.fn_get_audit_file using wildcard paths — not with grep — and you can filter by object name, event time, principal, and statement to answer compliance questions like 'who touched customer_payments last Tuesday'.
options: grep the .sqlaudit files for the table name.
Query sys.fn_get_audit_file with the audit file path pattern, filtering on event_time, object_name, and server_principal_name.
Read the SQL Server Error Log with sp_readerrorlog.
Restore the audit database from backup.
questions.q: An auditor asks: 'Who touched customer_payments last Tuesday?' How do you answer from SQL Server Audit output?

questions.explain: SERVER_ROLE_MEMBER_CHANGE_GROUP fires when someone is added to or removed from a fixed server role like sysadmin, and DATABASE_ROLE_MEMBER_CHANGE_GROUP covers database roles — the chapter calls these two non-negotiable for security auditing, paired with an alert since an unread audit record is just disk usage.
options: SUCCESSFUL_LOGIN_GROUP and FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP.
SERVER_ROLE_MEMBER_CHANGE_GROUP (and DATABASE_ROLE_MEMBER_CHANGE_GROUP) — they capture exactly who became sysadmin, and when.
LOGOUT_GROUP.
DATABASE_OBJECT_ACCESS_GROUP.
questions.q: Which audit action groups capture privilege escalation — e.g., who was made sysadmin and when?
